The standard quarter-wavelength multilayer coating has the highest reflectivity for a given number of layers, but does not necessarily yield the lowest thermal noise.
The optimized coating was designed by finding the configuration of layer thicknesses that minimized the Brownian noise of the coating as a whole, while maintaining the desired reflectance.
The optimized coating design consisted of 17 identical high/low index layer pairs or "doublets", with the exception of the terminal layers.

The material parameters used in the coating design were: silica (SiO2) Young's modulus Y = 72.0 GPa, Poisson ratio σ = 0.17, and loss angle φ = 2.1 × 10^-8; tantala (Ta2O5) Young's modulus Y = 140 GPa, Poisson ratio σ = 0.23, and loss angle φ = 4.7 × 10^-8.
The reflectance of the standard quarter-wavelength (QWL) coating was 0.9997225 (278 ppm transmittance).
The reflectance of the optimized coating was also 0.9997225, the same as the standard QWL coating.
The measured mean loss angle for the standard QWL coating was φ_QWL = (8.25 ± 0.35) × 10^-6.
The measured mean loss angle for the optimized coating was φ_opt = (6.85 ± 0.18) × 10^-6.
The ratio of the mean loss angles, r = φ_opt / φ_QWL, was 0.83, indicating an approximately 17% reduction in thermal noise for the optimized coating.
The thermal noise was measured over a frequency range of approximately 800 Hz to 20 kHz, above the unity gain frequency of the servos used in the thermal noise interferometer.
Above 20 kHz, the noise floor of the thermal noise interferometer became dominated by shot noise.
The researchers took multiple measurements for each coating and averaged the results to mitigate instability in the optical gains of the servos.
The distribution of residuals from the least-squares fits to the length noise data was consistent with a normal distribution, indicating the scatter was random in nature.
The researchers discarded a few anomalously high loss angle measurements that were likely due to transients affecting the noise floor of the instrument.
The thermal noise interferometer used short, independent arm cavities with suspended mirrors to optimize the system for measuring displacement noise.
